Moon :: History of scientific understanding and exploration :: Moon Treaty and explorational absence (1976–1990) :: chunk_0037
Main article: [Moon Treaty](/wiki/Moon_Treaty "Moon Treaty")

Following the [last Soviet mission to the Moon](/wiki/Luna_24 "Luna 24") of 1976, there was little further lunar exploration for fourteen years. Astronautics had shifted its focus towards the exploration of the [inner](/wiki/Inner_Solar_System "Inner Solar System") (e.g. [Venera program](/wiki/Venera_program "Venera program")) and [outer](/wiki/Outer_Solar_System "Outer Solar System") (e.g. [Pioneer 10](/wiki/Pioneer_10 "Pioneer 10"), 1972) [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") [planets](/wiki/Planet "Planet"), but also towards [Earth orbit](/wiki/Geocentric_orbit "Geocentric orbit"), developing and continuously operating, beside [communication satellites](/wiki/Communication_satellite "Communication satellite"), [Earth observation satellites](/wiki/Earth_observation_satellite "Earth observation satellite") (e.g. [Landsat program](/wiki/Landsat_program "Landsat program"), 1972), [space telescopes](/wiki/Space_telescope "Space telescope") and particularly [space stations](/wiki/Space_station "Space station") (e.g. [Salyut program](/wiki/Salyut_program "Salyut program"), 1971).

Negotiation in 1979 of [Moon treaty](/wiki/Moon_treaty "Moon treaty"), and its subsequent ratification in 1984 was the only major activity regarding the Moon until 1990.

[Photochrom](/wiki/Photochrom "Photochrom") of Monaco circa 1900

Until the [Monégasque Revolution](/wiki/Mon%C3%A9gasque_Revolution "Monégasque Revolution") of 1910 forced the adoption of the 1911 [Constitution of Monaco](/wiki/Constitution_of_Monaco "Constitution of Monaco"), the [princes of Monaco](/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Monaco "List of rulers of Monaco") were [absolute rulers](/wiki/Absolute_monarchy "Absolute monarchy").[[42]](#cite_note-45) The new constitution slightly reduced the autocratic rule of the Grimaldi family and [Prince Albert I](/wiki/Albert_I,_Prince_of_Monaco "Albert I, Prince of Monaco") suspended it during the First World War.

In July 1918, a new [Franco-Monégasque Treaty](/wiki/Franco-Mon%C3%A9gasque_Treaties "Franco-Monégasque Treaties") was signed, providing for limited French protection over Monaco. The treaty, endorsed in 1919 by the [Treaty of Versailles](/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles "Treaty of Versailles"), established that Monégasque international policy would be aligned with French political, military and economic interests. It also resolved the [Monaco succession crisis](/wiki/Monaco_succession_crisis_of_1918 "Monaco succession crisis of 1918").

The [Ohio Union](/wiki/Ohio_Union "Ohio Union") was the first [student union](/wiki/Student_center "Student center") at a state university in the United States.[[47]](#cite_note-What_was_the_first_student_union-48)

Ohio State's 1,764-acre (7.14 km2) main campus is about 2.5 miles (4.0 km) north of Columbus' downtown. The historical center of campus is the Oval, a [quad](/wiki/Quadrangle_(architecture) "Quadrangle (architecture)") of about 11 acres (4.5 ha).[[48]](#cite_note-faqs-49) The original campus was laid out in the English country style with University Hall overlooking what would become the Oval. From 1905 to 1913, the [Olmsted brothers](/wiki/Olmsted_Brothers "Olmsted Brothers"), who had designed New York City's [Central Park](/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park"), were contracted as architectural consultants. Under their leadership, a more formal landscape plan was created with its center axis through the Oval. This axis shifted the university's street grid 12.25 degrees from the City of Columbus' street grid. Construction of the main library in 1915 reinforced this grid shift.[[49]](#cite_note-50)

Ohio State's [research library](/wiki/Research_library "Research library") system has a combined collection of over 5.8 million volumes. Along with 21 libraries on its Columbus campus, the university has eight branches at off-campus research facilities and regional campuses, and a book storage depository near campus. In all, the Ohio State library system encompasses 55 branches and specialty collections. fanoutqa_035119.x:
Brooklyn Technical High School :: History :: chunk_0003
In 1918, Dr. Albert L. Colston, chair of the Math Department at Manual Training High School, recommended establishing a technical high school for Brooklyn boys. His plan envisioned a heavy concentration of [math](/wiki/Math "Math"), science, and [drafting](/wiki/Technical_drawing "Technical drawing") courses with parallel paths leading either to college or to a technical career in industry. By 1922, Dr. Colston's concept was approved by the Board of Education, and Brooklyn Technical High School opened in a converted warehouse at 49 [Flatbush Avenue](/wiki/Flatbush_Avenue "Flatbush Avenue") Extension, with 2,400 students. This location, in the shadow of the [Manhattan Bridge](/wiki/Manhattan_Bridge "Manhattan Bridge"), is the reason the school seal bears that bridge's image, rather than the more obvious symbol for the borough, the [Brooklyn Bridge](/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge "Brooklyn Bridge"). Brooklyn Tech would occupy one more location before settling into its site at 29 [Fort Greene](/wiki/Fort_Greene "Fort Greene") Place, for which the groundbreaking was held in 1930.[[8]](#cite_note-9)
